title: Choosing what to train
summary: Fine-tuning methods differ primarily in which degrees of freedom they allow an optimizer to change.

sections.title: A pretrained model is a starting point
paragraphs: Full fine-tuning updates the existing model weights. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes most of those weights and introduces or selects a smaller trainable parameter set. Both methods still require suitable data, a loss, and validation. Freezing parameters is a constraint on optimization, not a guarantee against overfitting or forgetting. A small adapter can alter the model's behavior substantially because its outputs pass through many subsequent nonlinear layers.

sections.title: Follow the memory, not just the weights
paragraphs: A trainable parameter may require a gradient and optimizer state in addition to its stored value. Freezing it can remove these training allocations, but the frozen weights must still be available during the forward pass. Backpropagation through frozen layers may also be necessary to reach earlier trainable components. Consequently, activation memory often remains substantial. Record parameter, optimizer, and activation memory separately before predicting whether a method will fit on your GPU.

sections.title: Make a controlled comparison
paragraphs: Imagine a 100-million-parameter backbone and a one-million-parameter adapter. The adapter stores only \(1\%\) as many trainable parameters, but that does not imply a 100-fold reduction in total GPU memory or runtime. Compare methods with the same examples, evaluation prompts, and validation procedure. Tune learning rates separately: restricting the trainable space changes optimization. If full tuning wins, investigate whether capacity, target layers, or training budget explains the difference before attributing it to the method alone.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read the LoRA and bottleneck-adapter papers through the question of what is allowed to change. Draw the frozen backbone in one color and the trainable components in another. An inserted nonlinear adapter and a factorized update to an existing projection occupy different places in that graph, even when their trainable parameter counts are similar. Their small checkpoint sizes therefore do not establish equivalent models.

For each trainable component, trace its influence on the loss backward through the graph. If an early adapter affects a later frozen layer's input, that layer can still participate in differentiation. This explains why freezing weights and eliminating all backward computation are different operations. Build a resource table with separate rows for stored weights, gradients, optimizer state, and activations. When a paper reports efficiency, identify which rows were measured and under what batch and sequence lengths before translating a parameter-count reduction into a hardware requirement.

exercise.prompt: A model has 100 million frozen parameters and 2 million trainable adapter parameters. What fraction of its total parameters is trainable?
exercise.answer: \(\frac{2}{102}\approx1.96\%\). This is a parameter fraction, not a prediction of the fraction of training memory or compute used.

takeaways: Trainable parameter count describes optimization freedom.
Measure complete memory and task quality under matched conditions.

title: Why a low-rank update can be useful
summary: LoRA constrains the change to a weight matrix rather than assuming the pretrained matrix itself has low rank.

sections.title: The change may be simpler than the model
paragraphs: A pretrained linear map can encode many capabilities while a particular adaptation needs only a few coordinated changes. LoRA explores this possibility by representing the update as a product of two thin matrices. It is an inductive bias: useful updates might concentrate in a smaller subspace. It is not a theorem that every task admits an accurate low-rank solution, nor does it require the original weights to be low rank.

sections.title: Think in input and output directions
paragraphs: Let \(A\) have \(r\) rows and let \(B\) have \(r\) columns. \(A\) extracts \(r\) learned combinations of input features; \(B\) maps those combinations into the output space. The resulting update cannot have rank greater than \(r\). For a \(4\times4\) matrix, a rank-one update can be written as an outer product \(uv^\mathsf{T}\). Every input correction is a scalar multiple of the same output direction \(u\), although the scalar depends on the input through \(v\).

sections.title: Diagnose a capacity restriction
paragraphs: Suppose the desired change independently boosts two unrelated feature directions. One rank-one update may not represent that change exactly; rank two could. In a deep network, however, several low-rank updates interact with nonlinearities, so local rank is not the rank of the complete model's behavioral change. A practical diagnostic is to sweep rank while holding data fixed, track validation performance, and inspect update singular values. A flat curve might indicate adequate rank, weak training signal, or poor target-layer selection.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: The central object to inspect in LoRA is the weight change, not a compressed replacement for the original matrix. Rewrite the paper's factorization using a small square example and identify the input directions selected by \(A\) and the output directions supplied by \(B\). This turns a storage formula into a statement about which linear corrections can be represented.

Now construct a diagonal target update with three nonzero diagonal entries and ask whether rank two can reproduce it exactly. It cannot, but that matrix example alone does not predict the quality of a deep model adapted with many rank-two updates. Read empirical rank investigations with that distinction in mind: an observed low-rank solution on selected tasks is evidence about those adaptations, not a universal theorem. Useful follow-up measurements include singular values of learned updates and validation performance across ranks, while keeping scale, target locations, and optimization choices visible.

exercise.prompt: Can a rank-one update transform the \(2\times2\) zero matrix into the identity matrix?
exercise.answer: No. The identity has rank two, while any outer product has rank at most one. Two independent rank-one terms can represent it.

takeaways: Low rank constrains \(\Delta W\), not the pretrained \(W\).
Local matrix rank is only one part of a deep model's effective capacity.

title: Deriving the LoRA forward pass
summary: Two small trainable matrices add an adjustable correction to a frozen linear projection.

sections.title: Choose a shape convention first
paragraphs: Use column vectors to define a linear layer \(y=Wx\), with \(W\) shaped \(d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}\). Introduce \(A\) shaped \(r\times d_{\text{in}}\) and \(B\) shaped \(d_{\text{out}}\times r\). The adapter first compresses \(x\) to \(r\) values and then expands it to \(d_{\text{out}}\) values. A scalar multiplier controls the correction. The base matrix remains frozen, while gradients update \(A\) and \(B\). Bias handling is a separate implementation choice and should be stated explicitly.

sections.title: Compute the two paths
paragraphs: The effective matrix is \(W'=W+sBA\), where standard LoRA uses \(s=\frac{\alpha}{r}\). During training there is no need to materialize \(BA\): compute \(Wx\) and \(sB(Ax)\), then add them. For a batch using row vectors \(X\) with shape \([\text{batch},d_{\text{in}}]\), the same operation is \(XW^\mathsf{T}+s(XA^\mathsf{T})B^\mathsf{T}\). Both paths produce \([\text{batch},d_{\text{out}}]\). Confusing the column-vector derivation with row-vector tensor code is a common source of transposition errors.

sections.title: Count and test a small layer
paragraphs: Take \(d_{\text{in}}=8\), \(d_{\text{out}}=6\), and \(r=2\). Full matrix adaptation has 48 trainable values; the two adapter matrices have \(16+12=28\), a saving. The break-even rank is \(\frac{d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}}{d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}}=\frac{48}{14}\approx3.43\). Rank 4 would require 56 adapter values, exceeding the full matrix's 48. Tiny layers leave little room for parameter-efficient ranks. Test the implementation by comparing the two-path output with the output of an explicitly merged matrix using fixed weights and dropout disabled. The outputs should agree within numerical tolerance, and frozen \(W\) should receive no parameter gradient.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: When reading LoRA's forward equation, translate every symbol into the tensor convention used by your code. A paper may multiply column vectors on the right of a matrix, while a framework stores a batch as rows. Write the same operation both ways and mark the two transposes explicitly. The low-rank branch must end with exactly the same output shape as the frozen branch.

Use a non-square layer for an independent check, because equal input and output widths can hide an incorrect transpose. Choose \(d_{\text{in}}=5\), \(d_{\text{out}}=3\), and \(r=2\), then compare the two-path computation with an explicitly formed effective matrix. Also verify the parameter count: the adapter contains \(10+6\) values rather than the full matrix's 15, so this tiny example is not parameter-efficient. The paper's motivation concerns suitable ranks relative to large dimensions; the algebra alone does not guarantee savings for every layer.

exercise.prompt: For \(d_{\text{in}}=d_{\text{out}}=1024\) and \(r=8\), how many adapter parameters are trained, excluding biases?
exercise.answer: \(8\times1024+1024\times8=16{,}384\), compared with \(1{,}048{,}576\) parameters in the full matrix: \(\frac{1}{64}\) as many.

takeaways: Write tensor shapes before implementing the two linear paths.
A merged-matrix comparison is a direct check of the forward equation.

title: Tuning rank, scale, and adapter dropout
summary: Rank controls available update directions, while scaling and dropout change how those directions are trained.

sections.title: Three knobs with different jobs
paragraphs: Rank \(r\) sets the width of the adapter bottleneck. Scaling \(\alpha\) changes the magnitude of its contribution through \(s=\frac{\alpha}{r}\) in standard LoRA. Adapter dropout randomly masks elements of the adapter input during training; the frozen base path is normally unaffected. Increasing rank therefore changes both capacity and, if \(\alpha\) is held fixed, the explicit scale. A rank experiment that ignores this coupling can confuse optimization effects with capacity effects.

sections.title: Separate magnitude from regularization
paragraphs: With \(r=8\) and \(\alpha=16\), \(s\) equals 2. With \(r=32\) and the same \(\alpha\), \(s\) equals 0.5. This calculation does not predict the final update norm because learned \(A\) and \(B\) can change their magnitudes, but it does affect the training dynamics. Inverted dropout with probability \(p\) keeps values with probability \(1-p\) and rescales surviving values by \(\frac{1}{1-p}\), preserving their expectation. It is disabled for deterministic evaluation.

sections.title: Design a readable sweep
paragraphs: Start with a small rank grid and record rank, \(\alpha\), dropout, learning rate, target modules, and validation score. Also log the norm of the effective update relative to the base weight. If a larger rank performs worse, check learning rate and scaling before concluding that capacity is harmful. Excessive dropout may make a small dataset harder to fit, while too little regularization may encourage memorization. Always compare in evaluation mode; stochastic adapter dropout can otherwise disguise reproducibility problems.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Place the original LoRA scaling convention beside the rsLoRA paper's alternative. The useful reading question is what changes when rank changes while the user-facing \(\alpha\) stays fixed. Compute both multipliers for a sequence of ranks before looking at an empirical curve. Otherwise a curve labeled only by rank may combine a capacity change with a substantially different update scale.

To investigate the distinction, keep a record of initialization, learning rate, dropout, and the norm of the effective update. Equal explicit multipliers do not guarantee equal learned norms, because the optimization trajectories also change. Dropout introduces another source of randomness on the adapter path, so compare evaluation outputs with that randomness disabled. A careful paper reading separates the mathematical parameterization from claims about training stability and from measured downstream quality. Treat the proposed scaling as a hypothesis to test under a documented configuration, rather than as evidence that rank can be increased without any resource or optimization consequences.

exercise.prompt: You double both \(r\) and \(\alpha\) in standard LoRA. What happens to the explicit multiplier, and what still changes?
exercise.answer: \(\frac{\alpha}{r}\) stays constant. The number of trainable parameters and maximum update rank increase, so the optimization problem and potential capacity still change.

takeaways: Rank, \(\alpha\), and learning rate interact.
Dropout is a training regularizer, not an inference compression method.

title: Where to insert LoRA
summary: The choice of target projections determines which computations an adapter can directly modify.

sections.title: Attention has several intervention points
paragraphs: Adapting \(Q\) or \(K\) directly changes attention scores and therefore which positions can influence a token. Adapting \(V\) changes the information carried along those attention weights. Adapting \(O\) changes how head outputs are mixed back into the residual stream. An MLP adapter instead changes token-wise feature transformations after attention. These are functional descriptions, not guarantees that a trained adapter will specialize cleanly in only one role.

sections.title: Account for unequal projection shapes
paragraphs: In multi-head attention, projection widths are often similar, but grouped-query attention may use narrower \(K\) and \(V\) projections. For any target matrix, LoRA contributes \(r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})\) parameters. A fixed rank across every target therefore does not allocate an equal parameter budget to every component. Gated MLPs also contain several matrices, usually with a much wider intermediate dimension. Count each actual tensor rather than estimating from module names or assuming a single FFN matrix.

sections.title: Compare coverage at a fixed budget
paragraphs: Consider a layer with four \(512\times512\) attention projections. Rank 4 on all four uses \(16{,}384\) parameters; rank 8 on just \(Q\) and \(V\) uses the same number. The two choices offer different adaptation paths even though their budget matches. Run an ablation using identical training examples and evaluate several task types. A common implementation error is targeting a name that does not exist in the selected architecture. Inspect named modules and the final trainable parameter list before launching a long run.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: The target-matrix experiments in LoRA are useful because they ask where a limited adaptation budget should be spent. Inspect which projections are changed in each condition and recalculate the number of adapter values. Two configurations with the same nominal rank can have different budgets if they cover different matrices; two configurations with matching budgets can intervene in very different computations.

Connect those experiments to a single attention head. A change to \(Q\) or \(K\) can alter its attention distribution, while a change to \(V\) can alter what information is aggregated under an unchanged distribution. In a full network these roles interact, so the distinction is a way to design an ablation rather than a promise of isolated behavior. Consult the PEFT target-module reference only after checking the actual checkpoint's module names and shapes. A published architectural label does not establish that a string such as q_proj exists in every implementation.

exercise.prompt: A projection is \(256\times1024\) and uses rank 4. How many LoRA parameters does it add?
exercise.answer: \(4(1024+256)=5{,}120\). A square \(1024\times1024\) target at the same rank would add \(8{,}192\).

takeaways: Target modules define where adaptation enters the computation.
Compare target coverage and rank under an explicit parameter budget.

title: Initializing, merging, and restoring LoRA
summary: A correct LoRA implementation can begin as the base model and later fold its learned update into a linear weight.

sections.title: Start with a zero correction
paragraphs: A common initialization draws \(A\) randomly and sets \(B\) to zero. Then \(BA\) is zero, so adding the adapter initially preserves the base layer's output. The two matrices should not both start at zero: the gradients of their product would then vanish for both. With \(B\) initially zero, \(B\) can receive a useful first gradient through the nonzero \(A\); \(A\) generally begins receiving a nonzero gradient after \(B\) changes. Other initialization schemes exist, so check the actual configuration.

sections.title: Merging is an algebraic operation
paragraphs: With dropout disabled and fixed adapter weights, replace \(W\) by \(W+sBA\) to obtain the same linear function without separate adapter matrix multiplications. Unmerging subtracts that same update if the implementation retains it. Repeated add/subtract operations in low precision can accumulate rounding error. A merged copy is therefore best treated as a deployment artifact, while the original backbone and adapter checkpoint remain the reliable sources for further training or changing adapters.

sections.title: Test the lifecycle explicitly
paragraphs: On a small FP32 layer, save base weights, compute an unmerged evaluation output, merge once, and compare outputs. Then restore the saved base weights and compare again. Do not merge twice: that would add two copies of the update. Quantized backbones need additional care because dequantization, addition, and requantization can introduce error or may be unsupported in a particular library path. Finally, an adapter checkpoint alone usually depends on the exact base model revision; record that revision with the artifact.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read LoRA's initialization and merging discussion together. A zero initial correction must preserve the base function while still permitting a learning signal to enter one factor. Write the gradients of \(B(Ax)\) for a scalar loss and substitute \(B=0\). This reveals why one factor can begin learning before the other, and why setting both factors to zero is a different situation.

Then separate mathematical merging from a library operation. The identity \(W_{\text{merged}}=W+sBA\) assumes the same adapter weights, the same scale, and a deterministic linear path. A checkpoint may also contain trained biases or other modules, which must not disappear from the deployment artifact. In the PEFT reference, inspect whether an operation retains adapter state or returns a model without it. Test a saved base-plus-adapter pair independently of any merged copy. Numerical agreement should be measured with a stated tolerance, particularly when the deployment path changes precision.

exercise.prompt: Why does initializing both \(A\) and \(B\) to zero prevent the first update under the usual LoRA parameterization?
exercise.answer: The gradient with respect to \(A\) contains \(B\), and the gradient with respect to \(B\) contains \(A\). If both are zero, both gradients are zero.

takeaways: A zero initial update should still allow gradients to flow.
Keep the base model and adapter artifact when creating a merged deployment model.

title: Adapters, prefixes, and soft prompts
summary: Parameter-efficient methods differ in whether they alter hidden transformations, attention context, or the input sequence.

sections.title: Locate the trainable component
paragraphs: A bottleneck adapter typically inserts a small down-projection, nonlinearity, and up-projection into a network, often with a residual connection. Prompt tuning learns continuous embeddings prepended to the input. Prefix tuning learns continuous conditioning that supplies additional attention context, commonly represented through per-layer key/value prefixes. None of these learned vectors must correspond to readable words. Their location matters: equal parameter counts do not imply identical access to the model's internal computations.

sections.title: Compare the shapes and costs
paragraphs: For hidden width \(d\) and bottleneck \(b\), a simple adapter uses roughly \(2db\) matrix parameters, ignoring biases. An input soft prompt of length \(m\) uses \(md\) values. A direct key/value prefix with \(m\) positions across \(L\) layers can require roughly \(2Lmd\) values before accounting for head layouts or reparameterization. Prefixes and prompts may increase attention sequence length or cache use, while inserted adapters add extra layer operations. These runtime effects differ from merging a linear LoRA correction into existing weights.

sections.title: Choose based on the task interface
paragraphs: Suppose a frozen model must support many small task-specific packages. A soft prompt is compact and easy to select, but it spends context positions and may be sensitive to initialization and model scale. An adapter can intervene deeper but requires modifying the network. A prefix can condition multiple layers without updating the backbone. Evaluate task quality, storage, context budget, and serving complexity together. Calling every method a prompt obscures these practical differences and can lead to loading a checkpoint into the wrong architecture.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Compare the adapter, prefix-tuning, and prompt-tuning sources by drawing the location of their learned values. For each, ask whether those values modify a hidden transformation, provide attention keys and values, or enter as input embeddings. This makes the papers' shared goal of compact adaptation easier to understand without collapsing their distinct mechanisms into a single category.

Use a fixed hidden width and a small parameter budget to work out feasible bottleneck sizes or prompt lengths. Then identify costs that the count misses: extra sublayer operations, added context positions, and cached prefix tensors. The direct key/value-prefix estimate in this article is only a shape model; implementations may learn a reparameterization and use attention-head layouts that change the stored tensors. When reading reported transfer results, note model scale and task interface. A compact package that works well for generation need not provide the same intervention for a token-labeling head or a spatial vision task.

exercise.prompt: For \(d=768\) and \(m=20\), how many parameters does an input-only soft prompt contain?
exercise.answer: \(20\times768=15{,}360\). This excludes the frozen language model and is not the count for a separate key/value prefix at every layer.

takeaways: Identify where the trainable component enters the network.
Small checkpoints can still add inference computation or context overhead.

title: Training LoRA on a quantized backbone
summary: QLoRA saves backbone storage while allowing gradients to train higher-precision adapter parameters.

sections.title: Separate storage from arithmetic
paragraphs: A four-bit backbone stores weights using quantized codes and associated metadata. Computation generally uses dequantized or fused representations in a higher-precision arithmetic path. The quantized base weights remain frozen, while LoRA matrices are trainable. Calling the entire operation four-bit training is therefore misleading: activations, gradients, adapters, and optimizer state need their own precision choices. Quantization primarily changes how the large frozen weight collection is represented in memory.

sections.title: Follow one gradient path
paragraphs: For a linear layer, the forward computation combines the approximate base projection with a trainable adapter correction. The loss gradient reaches \(A\) and \(B\) through that correction. It can also propagate through frozen backbone operations to earlier adapters without updating the base weight codes. Freezing a parameter does not remove the need to compute gradients with respect to its input. This distinction explains why adapter training still has substantial activation and backward-pass costs.

sections.title: Estimate before measuring
paragraphs: A hypothetical one-billion-parameter backbone needs \(0.5\,\text{GB}\) for four-bit codes alone, compared with \(2\,\text{GB}\) for two-byte weights, using decimal units. Real memory exceeds those figures because quantization scales, adapters, activations, temporary buffers, and optimizer states also occupy space. Quantization can change model outputs, so compare the frozen quantized baseline before attributing any quality loss to LoRA training. Check supported kernels, compute dtype, gradient checkpointing, and the exact preparation procedure for the chosen library version. A memory-saving setup is not automatically faster on every device.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: QLoRA combines a frozen quantized backbone with trainable adaptation; read its memory discussion by separating storage representation from the arithmetic used in a layer. On a diagram, label the quantized codes, reconstruction metadata, adapter tensors, and activations. Only then identify which quantities the optimizer can update. Calling all of these objects four-bit values would obscure the method's actual resource trade-off.

For an independent experiment, compare three states: the original frozen model, its quantized frozen counterpart, and that counterpart after adapter training. This isolates a quantization effect from the effect of adaptation. Measure peak memory during a full step, not just immediately after loading weights, because backward activations and temporary buffers can dominate the missing difference. In the PEFT documentation, check the supported preparation and compute-dtype choices for the installed versions. A paper's successful configuration establishes a concrete result, while a particular device and kernel combination still needs its own measurement.

exercise.prompt: Can QLoRA update the frozen four-bit base codes through its usual optimizer step?
exercise.answer: No. The optimizer updates the adapter parameters and any explicitly trainable extra modules. Backpropagation through the backbone does not imply that its quantized codes are optimized.

takeaways: Quantized storage and compute precision are different choices.
Track all memory components, including backward activations.

title: What NF4 and double quantization store
summary: Weight quantization compresses both weight values and the metadata needed to reconstruct approximate values.

sections.title: A codebook replaces exact values
paragraphs: Four bits provide sixteen possible codes, not sixteen uniformly spaced real numbers by necessity. NF4 uses a nonuniform codebook motivated by approximately normal weight distributions. A block scale maps a group of weights into the range represented by that codebook. Values near densely populated regions receive finer resolution than uniformly spaced codes would provide. The statistical motivation is useful, but a real layer can contain outliers and need not follow the assumed distribution exactly.

sections.title: Metadata has a cost too
paragraphs: Quantizing a block requires recording information such as its scale. If a 64-weight block stores sixteen possible codes per weight and one FP32 scale, the simple accounting is \(4+\frac{32}{64}=4.5\) bits per weight, excluding other metadata. Double quantization compresses these quantization constants as well. It does not apply another arbitrary four-bit quantizer to an already four-bit weight and somehow produce four squared bits of information. The second stage targets metadata overhead.

sections.title: Inspect reconstruction error by layer
paragraphs: Take a tiny block containing several small weights and one unusually large weight. A shared scale chosen to cover the outlier can reduce precision for the small values. Smaller blocks may localize that effect but require more scales. Compare mean squared reconstruction error, maximum error, and downstream output error, since a numerically small error in a sensitive direction can matter. Do not assume lower average weight error always means better task accuracy. Evaluate the quantized model with the same tokenizer, prompts, and decoding settings as the unquantized reference.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: The NF4 and double-quantization discussion in QLoRA is easiest to read as two separate encoding problems. First, approximate weight values with a small codebook and a block scale. Second, reduce the storage occupied by those scales. Sketch a byte-level record for one toy block so that the weight codes and their metadata cannot be accidentally counted as the same thing.

Now vary the block size while keeping the number of weights fixed. Larger blocks require fewer scales, but one outlier can influence more reconstructed values. The resulting trade-off concerns both error and metadata overhead; four-bit code storage alone is an incomplete memory estimate. Examine the paper's normal-distribution motivation as a design assumption, not a claim that every layer exactly follows that distribution. A useful extension is to compare errors before and after a linear projection, because two quantizers with similar weight reconstruction error can perturb task-relevant output directions differently.

exercise.prompt: With four-bit codes, one 16-bit scale per block, and 32 weights per block, what is the simple storage estimate?
exercise.answer: \(4+\frac{16}{32}=4.5\) bits per weight, before alignment and any additional metadata. The scale contributes 0.5 bits per weight.

takeaways: NF4 is a nonuniform representation with a statistical design assumption.
Double quantization reduces metadata storage rather than eliminating it.

title: What rsLoRA and DoRA change
summary: rsLoRA revisits rank-dependent scaling, while DoRA separates a weight's magnitude from its direction.

sections.title: Two different limitations
paragraphs: A larger adapter rank changes both the number of directions and how the update is scaled. rsLoRA addresses the scaling issue by using a square-root rank denominator rather than the standard rank denominator. DoRA addresses a different question: how should a model change the direction and magnitude of its weights? It represents these aspects separately, using a low-rank update for the directional component and trainable magnitudes. They are distinct modifications, not interchangeable names for increasing rank.

sections.title: Write each parameterization explicitly
paragraphs: For rsLoRA, the adapter multiplier is \(\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt r}\). With \(\alpha=16\) and \(r=64\), that multiplier is 2; standard \(\frac{\alpha}{r}\) would be 0.25. For a conceptual DoRA weight vector, write \(w'=m\frac{v+\Delta v}{\lVert v+\Delta v\rVert}\). The normalization isolates a direction, while \(m\) controls length. Actual matrix implementations must specify which axis defines a weight vector and how norms are computed. A zero or tiny norm needs numerically careful handling. In the paper's matrix convention, \(V\) starts at \(W_0\) and \(m\) at \(W_0\)'s column norms, so zero \(BA\) preserves the initial weight for nonzero columns. Its memory-saving variant detaches the norm denominator from backpropagation while recomputing its value in each forward pass. The forward expression is unchanged, but the gradients differ.
sections.formula: \begin{aligned}\text{rsLoRA:}\quad&\Delta W=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt r}BA\\\text{vector-form DoRA:}\quad&w'=m\frac{v+\Delta v}{\lVert v+\Delta v\rVert}\end{aligned}

sections.title: Compare without hiding the changed budget
paragraphs: DoRA introduces magnitude parameters and normalization work; rsLoRA changes the explicit scaling convention. Keep a record of these changes when comparing against a LoRA baseline. Reusing one learning rate across all variants is a convenience, not proof of a fair optimum. Measure validation quality, update norms, peak memory, and deployment behavior. Neither method establishes that full fine-tuning is always unnecessary. Their usefulness depends on model, target layers, data, rank, and optimization settings, which should remain visible in the experiment report.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read rsLoRA and DoRA as answers to different questions. The first revisits how an adapter's contribution scales with rank. The second separates magnitude from direction in the adapted weight. Translate both into one explicit shape convention before combining them in an implementation; otherwise a changed scaling factor can be mistaken for the entire magnitude-direction method.

For DoRA, choose one weight vector and compute its norm, normalized direction, and reconstructed value. Perturb its direction without changing its assigned magnitude, then change only the magnitude. These are distinct degrees of freedom that ordinary matrix addition does not expose separately. The paper uses a matrix-axis convention, so check whether a framework's transposed storage makes the corresponding norm run over rows or columns. For rsLoRA, compare effective update norms at several ranks rather than merely checking \(\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt r}\) numerically. Neither exercise reproduces the papers' training results, but both can catch an incorrectly implemented parameterization.

exercise.prompt: At fixed \(\alpha\), how does the rsLoRA multiplier change when rank increases from 16 to 64?
exercise.answer: The denominator increases from 4 to 8, so the multiplier halves. Under standard \(\frac{\alpha}{r}\) scaling it would become one quarter as large.

takeaways: rsLoRA changes rank scaling; DoRA changes weight parameterization.
State the norm axis and training budget when implementing a variant.

title: Comparing LoRA with full fine-tuning fairly
summary: A useful comparison separates adaptation quality, optimization budget, storage, and actual runtime costs.

sections.title: Define the claim before the experiment
paragraphs: A claim about memory efficiency is different from a claim about best achievable quality. LoRA may fit a device that cannot hold full optimizer state, while full tuning may offer more freedom to adapt to a large domain shift. Conversely, restricting updates can help in a small-data setting. None of those outcomes follows solely from the number of trainable parameters. Decide whether your experiment fixes GPU capacity, training time, examples seen, or total optimization steps.

sections.title: Measure the whole training system
paragraphs: Include frozen weights, trainable weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers in the memory report. Keep token lengths and microbatch sizes visible because they strongly affect activation memory. Report throughput after warmup and synchronize device work around timing boundaries. A LoRA method that trains fewer values can still spend much of its time in the base model's forward and backward computations. Merged inference and unmerged inference should be reported separately when relevant.

sections.title: Read a result with competing constraints
paragraphs: Suppose full tuning scores 82 and LoRA scores 81 on the same held-out metric, while their peak memory is \(24\,\text{GB}\) and \(10\,\text{GB}\). That one-point difference may or may not justify the larger resource requirement. Repeat runs to estimate variability, inspect important subgroups, and check whether LoRA rank or targets were tuned adequately. Save the validation choices separately from the test result. A common mistake is comparing a well-tuned full model with a single default adapter configuration and interpreting the gap as a fundamental capacity limit.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Use LoRA and QLoRA to practice reading an efficiency claim with its denominator attached. Identify the backbone, adaptation configuration, precision, training data, and measured resource. A comparison of checkpoint sizes answers a different question from a comparison of peak training memory, and both differ from time to reach a target validation score. Put these outcomes in separate columns instead of combining them into a single claim of being cheaper.

Then reconstruct a matched comparison of your own. Give each method a documented hyperparameter search allowance, record the examples or tokens consumed, and evaluate with the same prompts and scoring rules. If one method cannot fit the chosen device, report that feasibility constraint directly rather than inventing a quality comparison for an unrun baseline. Interpret a small score gap alongside repeated-run variation and the size of the resource saving. The papers motivate this investigation; they do not remove the need to define the comparison you intend to make.

exercise.prompt: Method A scores \(80\pm2\) across seeds and method B scores \(81\pm2\). Is one run enough to claim B is better?
exercise.answer: No. The observed gap is small relative to run variability. Use repeated matched evaluations, uncertainty estimates, and task-relevant effect sizes before making that claim.

takeaways: Resource savings and quality claims require different measurements.
Treat hyperparameter search and seed variation as part of the comparison.

title: A minimal PEFT workflow you can audit
summary: Using a library safely means checking the actual trainable modules, saved artifacts, and evaluation behavior.

sections.title: Inspect the model before wrapping it
paragraphs: Load a supported backbone and tokenizer, record their revisions, and inspect the names and shapes of its linear modules. Decide which projections should receive adapters rather than copying target names from an unrelated architecture. Create a LoRA configuration with explicit rank, \(\alpha\), dropout, task type, and target modules. Wrap the model using the PEFT API, then inspect the trainable parameter count and names. This short audit catches missing targets and accidentally trainable backbone components.

sections.title: Train with a visible loss path
paragraphs: Prepare tokenized examples with appropriate labels and padding masks. For causal language modeling, decide whether loss covers all text or only the desired response tokens; the choice affects the learning objective. Run a single batch first and inspect the loss. With standard random-\(A\), zero-\(B\) initialization, the task-loss gradient for \(A\) is zero on the first backward pass; \(B\) can receive a nonzero gradient. After \(B\) changes, gradients can reach \(A\). Check finite gradients and the expected pattern for the actual initialization, data, and objective, rather than requiring every tensor to be nonzero. Check that the optimizer contains only intended parameters. Quantized workflows also require the supported preparation steps for the installed PEFT and Transformers versions.

sections.title: Reload before trusting the artifact
paragraphs: Save the adapter configuration and weights along with the exact base model identity, tokenizer configuration, and training settings. In a fresh process, reload the base and attach the saved adapter. In evaluation mode with fixed inputs, compare logits or deterministic outputs with the original trained instance. An adapter checkpoint generally does not contain the full backbone. If deployment needs merged weights, create that artifact separately and test it as well. A successful save call alone does not demonstrate that another machine can reproduce the model.

sections.title: Reading the paper and implementation guide
paragraphs: The PEFT quicktour is an executable interface guide, while the LoRA paper explains why the added factors define a restricted weight update. Read them side by side and connect configuration fields to mathematical objects: rank sets the factor width, \(\alpha\) contributes to scaling, and target modules identify where the correction enters. Treat example target names as architecture-dependent choices rather than universal strings.

A useful audit artifact is a compact manifest of trainable parameter names and shapes before the first optimizer step. Compare it with the intended targets, then save and reload an adapter on the same base revision in a fresh process. Check logits on fixed inputs before evaluating generated text, since sampling can hide small discrepancies or create differences without a checkpoint error. The documentation's successful save call establishes that files were written; your reload check establishes whether the intended computation was recovered. Quantized and merged deployment paths require separate checks because they can change numerical behavior.

exercise.prompt: Why can a saved adapter produce different answers after loading onto a different revision of the same named backbone?
exercise.answer: The adapter was optimized relative to particular base weights and interfaces. Changed base weights, tokenization, or templates alter its computation even if model dimensions still match.

takeaways: Audit names, shapes, gradients, and trainable counts before training.
Validate a fresh reload and record the exact base revision.
